newsitem.title: USA: Agriculture Dept rewarded Clinton backers - report.
newsitem.headline: Agriculture Dept rewarded Clinton backers - report.

text.p: A House report said Tuesday the Agriculture Department rewarded employees who donated to President Clinton's 1992 campaign and punished Republican supporters, but current and former officials denied the claim.

The report prepared for the House Agriculture subcommittee described on-the-job solicitation of campaign contributions at the deparment. It also said lists were compiled after the election of "reliable and competent Democrats" for promotion and those to be "removed...as soon as possible."
Two career employees at the department told a subcommittee hearing they were transferred to lower-profile jobs, apparently because they were on a "hit" list.

But Ron Blackley, chief of staff for former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy, denied allegations that he asked for lists of employees who deserved special consideration and those who should be squelched.
Farm Service Agency administrator Grant Buntrock also denied political affiliation was a crucial factor in job assignments in his agency. "You don't buy jobs for $50 or $100 (donations)," she said.

FSA is the successor of the agency under investigation for soliciting campaign contributions on the job in violation of federal law. Four men who were supervisors at the agency in 1992 pleaded guilty earlier this month to conspiracy to gather the money and to suggest who deserved special treatment when Clinton won.
"There is a correlation between those who solicited or contributed ... and their subsequent positions," said James Lager, the investigator who compiled the report.

Lager said seven of the 10 people who were temporarily assigned as area director or deputy director in 1993 had given $100 or more to Farmers and Ranchers '92, a political action committee. Most of the 18 people targeted for removal no longer hold those jobs, he said.

Agriculture employees Chris Niedermayer and Eric Shrader said they were told they were being transferred to different jobs because of politics. Shrader said was informed he was "associated with a Republican list."

Buntrock, Blackley and a half-dozen other appointees denied seeking "hit" lists or using them. Buntrock said he could not recall a meeting that he allegedly arranged as an opportunity for campaign donors to discuss possible employment-related benefits.
